intro: You already know that vowels can become weak when they do not receive the strong beat in a word.
Some words hide a quiet **a** before **l** in **-al**. In the pronunciations shown here, it makes the weak **schwa /ə/** sound followed by **l**.
Listen to these words in British English. The exact syllables can vary by speaker; follow the chosen recording in each activity.
weakVowelFeature.conclusion: Notice the **a** near the end. It does not make its strong letter sound; in these examples it sounds like /ə/ before **l**. In today's activity words, follow the highlighted reviewed **a** and its recording.

tips.heading: Detective Tip 1: Find the hidden A!

blocks.text: Look at **n a t u r a l**. In the clear three-syllable pronunciation, the last **a** has a weak /ə/ sound. In quicker speech, that ending may be even harder to hear.
**Detective trick:** A quiet ‘uhl’ ending has several possible spellings. In these words, remember **-al**.

tips.heading: Detective Tip 2: Look for the -ual pattern!

blocks.text: These words share the written **u-a-l** pattern:
The **a** before **l** is weak, but it still belongs in the spelling. The **u** is another vowel: listen to the chosen word recording to hear how it is said.
**Memory trick:** Picture the three-letter spelling pattern **U-A-L**.

tips.heading: Detective Tip 3: Ask the word's relatives!

blocks.text: Related words often keep the written **-al** or **-ual** pattern:
**Detective trick:** If you know **actual**, its spelling helps you remember **actually**. A relative can preserve a spelling even when it does not make the vowel clearer.

intro: You already know that **ar** can make a strong sound, as in **car**, **star** and **park**.
But at the end of some British English words, **-ar** becomes quiet and makes the **schwa /ə/** sound, like ‘uh’.
weakVowelFeature.conclusion: The final **-ar** is unstressed in these examples. It sounds quiet, but we still spell both letters.

tips.heading: Detective Tip 1: Listen for the lazy AR!

blocks.text: Say **sugar**. Can you hear the strong **ar** sound from **car**? The last syllable is unstressed, so its vowel sounds like a quiet **‘uh’** /ə/.
**Remember:** At the end of some words, **ar** whispers ‘uh’!

tips.heading: Detective Tip 2: Spot the -ular pattern!

blocks.text: Some words share the written ending **-ular**:
**Remember:** Spot **-ular**, spell **u-l-a-r**! This is a spelling pattern, not a claim that these words share one base family.

tips.heading: Detective Tip 3: Check -ilar and -iliar!

blocks.text: These endings look alike, but they are not spelt the same:
**Remember:** **similar** ends **i-l-a-r**; **familiar** has an extra **i**: **i-l-i-a-r**.

tips.heading: Detective Tip 4: Ask the word's relatives!

blocks.text: A related word can sometimes make a hidden vowel clearer: **popular → popularity**.
In British English **popular**, the final written **a** sounds like /ə/. In **popularity**, that **a** is heard more clearly as /æ/.
**Remember:** A word's relatives can provide a clue, but not every relative reveals the sound.

tips.heading: Detective Tip 5: Remember the tricky AR words!

blocks.text: Some words need extra spelling practice:
**Remember:** Even when **ar** whispers ‘uh’, we still write **ar**!

tips.heading: Detective Tip 6: Don't trust your ears!

blocks.text: These endings can all sound like a quiet ‘uh’ in British English:
One ends in **-ar**, one in **-er**, and one in **-or**. Sound alone cannot always tell you which spelling to choose.
**Remember:** Your ears hear the sound; spelling patterns, relatives and memory help you choose the letters!

pages.title: The Secret of the Quiet -et
pages.subtitle: When the ending looks like -et but sounds like “it”!

intro: Remember how vowels can become weaker when they are not in the strongest syllable of a word?
Sometimes a word ends with **-et**, but when we say it naturally, the ending sounds more like “it”.
Look at these words. Say them aloud and compare how they sound with how they are spelt.
conclusion: Your ears might tell you to write **-it**, but these words are actually spelt with **-et**!
The **e** has a weak vowel sound. It doesn't sound like the clear short **e** in **bed**.

tips.heading: Detective Tip 1 — Don't let the sound trick you!

blocks.text: **Detective trick:** The ending might sound like “it”, but it can be hiding an **e**!

tips.heading: Detective Tip 2 — Watch out for real -it endings!

blocks.text: Not every ending that sounds like “it” is spelt **-et**.
You cannot always work out the spelling just by listening. You must learn which ending belongs to each word.

pages.title: The Disguised E!
pages.subtitle: The E is pretending to be I!

intro: Sometimes, the letter **E** puts on an **I** disguise!
When we say words like **basket**, **jacket** and **rocket**, the ending sounds like “it”.
But underneath that sound, there's a hidden **E** in the spelling.
Picture this: A cheeky letter **E** wearing an **I** costume, with the real **E** peeking out underneath.
rule: Some words sound like they end in “it”, but they are spelt with **-et**.
The letter **E** is only pretending to sound like **I**!
weakVowelFeature.motto: “Sounds like IT? Don't forget, E might be hiding in ET!”

intro: You already know that **or** can make a strong sound, like in **fork**, **storm** and **short**.

weakVowelFeature.conclusion: Notice something? Even though we write **or**, we hear **“uh”** at the end!

tips.heading: Detective Tip 1: Look for someone doing something!

blocks.text: One of the best clues for spelling **-or** is that it sometimes means **a person who does something**.
Look at these words:
The ending **-or** can tell us who performs an action.
But be careful! **-er** can do exactly the same job, as in **teacher** and **painter**.
**Detective trick:** If a word names someone doing something, check whether it belongs to an **-or** spelling family.

tips.heading: Detective Tip 2: Look for the -ator family!

blocks.text: Some words share a special spelling pattern: **-ator**.
These words all end in **-ator**, with a weak **“uh”** sound at the very end.
**Memory trick:** Spot the **-ator** pattern and remember that its final sound is spelt **-or**.

tips.heading: Detective Tip 3: Ask the word's relatives!

blocks.text: Sometimes a word's family helps you remember its ending. Look at these examples:
Even when we add more letters, the **or** spelling stays the same.
Once you learn the spelling of a word, its relatives become easier to spell too!

tips.heading: Detective Tip 4: Some words are just OR words!

blocks.text: Not every word ending in **-or** names someone doing something. Look at these words:
Col**or**? **No!** In British English, we spell this **colour**.
These words need a little extra spelling memory.
**Detective trick:** Remember the ending as a visual pattern, not just by listening to its sound.

pages.title: The Secret of the Lazy e-
pages.subtitle: When initial E sounds quiet!

intro: You already know that **e** can make different sounds, as in **egg**, **me** and **even**.
But did you know that **e** has a secret? At the beginning of some words, it can become weak.
In these common British pronunciations, the first **e** sounds like a short **“ih”** /ɪ/. Another syllable gets the strong beat.
weakVowelFeature.conclusion: Notice something? The first **e** is quiet while another syllable sounds stronger. A weak vowel is not always the schwa /ə/; these British examples commonly start with /ɪ/.

tips.heading: Detective Tip 1: Find the strong beat!

blocks.text: Listen to these words and notice the strong syllable:
Try clapping once for each syllable and making the stressed syllable louder.
**Detective trick:** When the first syllable is quiet, listen carefully to its weak vowel before checking the written **e**.

tips.heading: Detective Tip 2: Look for the ex- spelling pattern!

blocks.text: Some words begin with **ex-**, where the **e** is weak:

Listen carefully to the beginning. The **e** is weak, but the **x** still makes its consonant sound. In a common British pronunciation, **explain** begins /ɪk/, with the short /ɪ/ vowel rather than a schwa /ə/.
**Detective trick:** Remember the **ex-** spelling pattern, but do not assume every weak vowel is a schwa.

tips.heading: Detective Tip 3: Look for word families!

blocks.text: Related words can help you remember the spelling of a weak initial **e**:
Pronunciation and stress may change as a word grows, but these families keep the first written **e**.
**Detective trick:** Find related words and look for the letters that stay the same!

tips.heading: Detective Tip 4: Beware of the sneaky short I!

blocks.text: A quiet first **e** is not necessarily a schwa. In common British pronunciations, these words begin with short /ɪ/:
The short /ɪ/ and schwa /ə/ can sound similar in quick speech.
**Memory trick:** Listen to the chosen recording, then use a spelling clue to remember the **e**.

tips.heading: Detective Tip 5: Don't trust your ears alone!

blocks.text: Compare the quiet first vowels in **e**vent, **a**bout and **o**ccasion. Their sounds are not necessarily the same, and each word begins with a different letter.
Your ears can help you find a weak vowel, but they cannot always tell you how to spell it.
That's why a spelling detective looks for **word families, spelling patterns and meaning**.

weakVowelFeature.rule: At the beginning of many British English words, an unstressed **e** is weak. In today's examples it commonly sounds like short **“ih”** **/ɪ/**, not schwa **/ə/**.
clues: **Find the strong beat!** The first syllable may be quiet.
**Look for word families!** Related words can help you remember the spelling.
**Watch out for short /ɪ/!** Not every weak initial **e** is a schwa.
weakVowelFeature.conclusion: Follow the chosen word recording and use spelling clues when the quiet vowel is hard to hear.
weakVowelFeature.motto: Hear the weak vowel, find the strong beat, remember the E!

tips.heading: Detective Tip 1: Find the strong beat!

blocks.text: Listen to these words and notice the strong syllable:
Try clapping once for each syllable and making the stressed syllable louder.

tips.heading: Detective Tip 2: Look for the ex- spelling pattern!

blocks.text: Some words begin with **ex-**, where the **e** is weak:

Listen carefully to the beginning. The **e** is weak, but the **x** still makes its consonant sound. In a common British pronunciation, **explain** begins /ɪk/, with the short /ɪ/ vowel rather than a schwa /ə/.

tips.heading: Detective Tip 3: Look for word families!

blocks.text: Related words can help you remember the spelling of a weak initial **e**:
Pronunciation and stress may change as a word grows, but these families keep the first written **e**.
**Detective trick:** Find related words and look for the letters that stay the same!

tips.heading: Detective Tip 4: Beware of the sneaky short I!

blocks.text: A quiet first **e** is not necessarily a schwa. In common British pronunciations, these words begin with short /ɪ/:
The short /ɪ/ and schwa /ə/ can sound similar in quick speech.
**Memory trick:** Listen to the chosen recording, then use a spelling clue to remember the **e**.

tips.heading: Detective Tip 5: Don't trust your ears alone!

blocks.text: Compare the quiet first vowels in **e**vent, **a**bout and **o**ccasion. Their sounds are not necessarily the same, and each word begins with a different letter.
Your ears can help you find a weak vowel, but they cannot always tell you how to spell it.
That's why a spelling detective looks for **word families, spelling patterns and meaning**.

pages.title: The Secret of the Lazy o-
pages.subtitle: When O sounds like “uh”!

intro: You already know that **o** can make different sounds, as in **orange**, **open** and **hot**.
But did you know that **o** has a secret? At the beginning of some words, it can become quiet.
When the first syllable is unstressed, its **o** can sound like a soft **“uh”** called the **schwa** /ə/.
weakVowelFeature.conclusion: Notice something? The first **o** is weak while another syllable gets the strong beat. **Observation** is a useful relative, but its first **o** has a different sound in common British pronunciation.

tips.heading: Detective Tip 1: Find the strong beat!

blocks.text: Say these words aloud and listen for the strongest syllable:

**Detective trick:** If the first **o** is quiet and sounds like “uh”, you may have found a schwa. An unstressed **o** does not always become a schwa; follow the chosen recording.

tips.heading: Detective Tip 2: Look for the double consonant!

blocks.text: Some words with a quiet initial **o** have two of the same consonant near the beginning:
Can you spot **cc**, **pp** and **ff**?
**Memory trick:** Some quiet-**o** words have a double consonant just after the first vowel. A double consonant alone does not prove there is a schwa.

tips.heading: Detective Tip 3: Ask the word's relatives!

blocks.text: A related word can help you remember the first written **o**:
The spelling may stay while the sound changes. For example, British **observe** starts with schwa /ə/, but **observation** starts with /ɒ/ and has secondary stress there.
**Detective trick:** If you are unsure which vowel to write, look for a related word you already know. Do not assume it has the same vowel sound.

**Detective trick:** Do not rely on the first letter alone. Listen for the vowel and find the stressed syllable.

Their different spellings show why hearing a weak vowel is not enough to choose its letter.

pages.title: The Mystery of the Disappearing Middle Vowel
pages.subtitle: When a vowel hides in the middle of a word!

intro: Some words have written **vowels** that are hard to hear in the middle.
An unstressed vowel may sound weak. In some pronunciations, its separate sound disappears when syllables are compressed.
Even when the sound fades, **the vowel letter stays in the spelling**. Listen to these everyday British examples. Pronunciations can vary; in the activities, follow the chosen recording.
weakVowelFeature.conclusion: Can you spot the hard-to-hear written vowels? The reviewed **different** recording for these lessons has three syllables. A two-syllable form from another speaker is a variation.

tips.heading: Detective Tip 1: The disappearing vowel trick!

blocks.text: Look at **f a m i l y**. In a three-syllable pronunciation, the middle vowel is weak: **FAM-uh-lee**. Some speakers compress the word to **FAM-lee**.
The written **i** remains in both cases, even when the middle vowel is not heard as a separate sound.
**Detective trick:** When a word sounds shorter than it looks, search for a hidden written vowel. Use the recording you are given when counting syllables.

tips.heading: Detective Tip 2: Find the strong beat!

blocks.text: Listen for the part with the strongest beat:
The other parts are less stressed. Their vowels may be quieter, sound like schwa /ə/, or, in some pronunciations, no longer form a separate syllable.
**Detective trick:** Find the strong beat, then investigate the quieter parts of the recorded word.

tips.heading: Detective Tip 3: Use your spelling voice!

blocks.text: Your **speaking voice** sounds natural. Your **spelling voice** deliberately says the written parts to help you remember every vowel:
The spelling voice is a memory trick, **not** a claim about how the word is normally pronounced.
**Memory trick:** Speak naturally, but spell every letter!

tips.heading: Detective Tip 4: Ask the word's relatives!

blocks.text: Sometimes a related word gives a weak vowel a clearer sound:
The written **a** in **human** is weak /ə/, but in **humanity** it becomes /æ/. The second written **o** in British **photograph** is weak /ə/, but in **photography** it is /ɒ/.
**Detective trick:** A verified relative may reveal a spelling clue. Not every family has a helpful sound change.

tips.heading: Detective Tip 5: Beware of the vowel traps!

blocks.text: These spellings include a vowel that can be easy to miss by ear:
**Detective trick:** Picture the whole word and check every vowel, even when the sound is weak or absent in a compressed pronunciation.

tips.heading: Detective Tip 6: Don't trust your ears alone!

blocks.text: A written middle vowel may make a quiet sound such as schwa /ə/, keep another unstressed vowel sound, or disappear as a separate sound in a compressed pronunciation.
These are different possibilities. The number of syllables comes from the chosen recording, not from the number of written vowel letters.
Spelling detectives use **sound, word families, spelling patterns and memory** together.
